threats.description: Cutting or shorting the loop wiring at an accessible junction disrupts the primary measurement output.
threats.likelihoodRationale: IF-1's exposure is physical, matching ATK-2's access exactly; loop wiring is typically more physically accessible than the sensing head itself.
threats.impactRationale: Safety impact is tempered to 1 by AS-4/AS-5 (a defined fault current is driven, not an undefined/held value). Availability impact is 3 (capped at AS-A3's availability objective) for the loss of the process signal / possible spurious trip. Integrity 2.
threats.classificationRationale: The 4-20 mA loop wiring's physical accessibility depends entirely on plant cabling/conduit/cabinet practice, not on anything the RL-100 itself controls; the device's own contribution (a defined fail-safe fault current per AS-4/AS-5) already caps the safety impact. Consistent with the existing 'transferred' status.
threats.deploymentConstraints: Requires the plant to physically protect the loop wiring (conduit, locked junction boxes/cabinets, tamper-evident routing) between the RL-100 and the control system.

threats.description: An attacker injects a specific in-range current directly onto the loop wiring, producing a believable-but-false reading that the device's own NE43 fault logic cannot distinguish from a real measurement.
threats.likelihoodRationale: Requires loop access plus knowledge to inject a plausible in-range current alongside the device's own drive; no loop-tamper-detection mechanism is documented.
threats.impactRationale: AS-4/AS-5's fail-safe behavior only reacts to a detected device fault; an externally injected in-range value is not such a fault, so the full AS-A3 safety/integrity objective applies.
threats.classificationRationale: An in-range current injected directly onto the loop is indistinguishable from a real measurement using the device's own NE43 fault logic; the only effective control is physically securing the wiring against injection, which is a plant/installation matter, not an RL-100 capability. Matches the existing acceptanceRationale ('owner needs to secure plant').
threats.deploymentConstraints: Requires the plant to physically secure the loop wiring and junction points against injection (locked cabinets, tamper-evident conduit, restricted access), consistent with the already-recorded acceptance rationale.

threats.likelihoodRationale: AS-7 explicitly states HART read access requires no authentication.
threats.impactRationale: Impact limited to AS-A4's confidentiality objective; no integrity/availability/safety exposure from a read-only path.
threats.classificationRationale: HART provides no lightweight authentication primitive compatible with basic master read access, and gating reads would break compatibility with standard HART masters; the RL-100 follows conventional HART instrumentation practice of leaving read-only telemetry unauthenticated. This is an industry-convention judgment call rather than a hard protocol constraint, and impact is already low (confidentiality only).
threats.deploymentConstraints: Requires the plant to restrict physical/electrical access to the HART loop (IF-2) if the disclosed measurement/diagnostic data is considered sensitive.

threats.likelihoodRationale: A write gate exists per AS-7. Likelihood is conservatively rated pending finalization of the exact mechanism; REQC003 mandates it be no weaker than the already-decided local HMI baseline (AS-2 credential model, AS-12 lockout), so this is tracked as a requirement to close, not assumed broken. An on-site attacker (ATK-2) or a maintenance-credential-holding insider (ATK-5) are both plausible regardless of which specific mechanism is ultimately chosen.

threats.classificationRationale: The write gate itself exists (AS-7); the exact authentication mechanism is a still-open RL-100 design decision, now bounded by REQC003's minimum security bar rather than left undefined.
threats.acceptanceRationale: plant owner has to secure the plant

threats.description: A device sharing the same RS-485 multidrop segment passively eavesdrops on Modbus RTU traffic; Modbus RTU has no source authentication or encryption.
threats.likelihoodRationale: AS-6 models IF-3 as a shared multidrop segment where other devices cannot automatically be assumed trusted; passive monitoring requires only bus access, no active technique.
threats.impactRationale: Purely passive monitoring only exposes confidentiality, bounded by AS-A5's confidentiality objective.
threats.classificationRationale: Modbus RTU provides no cryptographic source authentication or encryption at the protocol level; any device with physical access to the shared bus can passively read traffic regardless of how the RL-100 itself is implemented.
threats.deploymentConstraints: Requires the plant to restrict which devices are physically wired onto the shared RS-485 segment (trusted-devices-only bus membership, physical access control to the wiring) since the RL-100 cannot enforce this over Modbus RTU itself.

threats.description: A device on the same RS-485 segment responds to master requests in place of, or claiming to be, the RL-100, causing the master to trust falsified data as if it came from the real device.
threats.likelihoodRationale: Requires the co-located device to actively race or substitute for the real device's slave response, a more involved technique than passive monitoring, but Modbus RTU has no source authentication to prevent it.
threats.impactRationale: A trusted-looking but falsified response primarily undermines integrity of the data the master acts on; some availability impact from response conflicts. Bounded by AS-A5's objectives.
threats.classificationRationale: Modbus RTU has no mechanism for a slave to prove its identity or for a master to detect a substituted/impersonating responder; this is a protocol-level gap, not an RL-100 implementation flaw.
threats.deploymentConstraints: Requires the same bus-membership/physical-access restriction as T-7, plus any master-side response-plausibility checks (timing, sequence, redundant cross-checks) being the responsibility of the control system, not the RL-100.

costRationales.time: Effort required for this attack path.

threats.description: A device on the shared RS-485 segment injects or modifies Modbus RTU frames, including writes to the write-capable operational configuration registers (range, damping, output behavior), which AS-10 confirms are not gated by any device-level authentication.
threats.likelihoodRationale: AS-10 confirms Modbus write access to operational configuration registers has no device-level authentication gate (protection is expected from the plant/control-system environment, not the protocol); combined with AS-6's shared multidrop topology, any device on the bus can attempt this.
threats.impactRationale: Integrity impact reflects AS-A12 (config changes can alter measurement/output behavior per the configuration-storage assumption). Availability impact of 2 reflects that a rogue device injecting/altering traffic on a shared RS-485 segment can cause communication failures, collisions, invalid responses, or master timeouts, not just a single write. Safety bounded by AS-A5's objective.
threats.classificationRationale: The root cause is the protocol-limitation shared with T-7/T-17 (no source authentication on Modbus RTU), but AS-10 also confirms the RL-100 currently offers no product-level gate on Modbus writes at all (e.g. a local write-protect switch or requiring local HMI confirmation before applying a remote write) -- a capability the manufacturer could reasonably add. Until such a capability exists, meaningful risk reduction depends on both a possible future product mitigation and deployment-level bus protection, so responsibility is shared rather than purely protocol-limitation.
threats.deploymentConstraints: Requires the same bus-membership/physical-access restriction as T-7/T-17 (network segmentation, trusted-devices-only bus membership) until/unless a product-level write-protect or local-confirmation mechanism is added; this threat should be reassessed if such a product capability is implemented.

threats.likelihoodRationale: AS-9 confirms secure key storage is assumed present (STM32H7 built-in), which narrows but does not eliminate this risk per ATK-4's profile; secure boot/hardware root of trust are explicitly not assumed present. AS-17 now confirms the obvious extraction path (an open, unrestricted production debug port) is not intended to exist -- a lab attacker would instead need to defeat MCU readout protection itself (decapping, side-channel, glitch), which is the higher-skill scenario already reflected in the existing acceptance rationale.
threats.impactRationale: Impact bounded by AS-A13's confidentiality/integrity/availability objectives.
threats.classificationRationale: AS-9 confirms secure boot/hardware root of trust are not assumed present; that hardware-security posture is entirely within the manufacturer's control.

threats.title: Firmware update bypass or rollback

costRationales.time: Effort required for this attack path.
costRationales.exploitability: Technical difficulty once the attack surface is reached.
costRationales.window: How often a practical opportunity is available.
costRationales.detection: Likelihood that the attempt is detected or interrupted.

threats.description: Residual risk given the confirmed update-time mitigations.
threats.likelihoodRationale: AS-3 confirms both signature and version are checked and rollback is prevented, substantially lowering likelihood. AS-9 confirms secure boot/hardware root of trust are not assumed present, so bypassing the update-time checker via a lower-level path is still conceivable in principle; however AS-17 now confirms that path is not an open production debug port -- it would require defeating MCU readout protection (RDP) itself, an the selected SL-C 2 attacker profile-level hardware attack rather than routine debug access. AS-19 further confirms the bootloader performing the update-time checks is itself stored in a write-protected flash region and is not modifiable through the normal update path, closing the lowest-effort variant of this threat (silently overwriting the bootloader/checker itself). Likelihood lowered from 3 to 2 and exposure factor reduced accordingly to reflect that the previously assumed-open low-effort avenue is now a design objective to be closed; the remaining, harder bypass-of-protection scenarios (debug access, fault injection, compromised manufacturing/provisioning) are tracked separately as T-22.
threats.impactRationale: Impact bounded by AS-A10's objectives.
threats.classificationRationale: Same driver as T-11 (AS-9's absence of secure boot/hardware root of trust); the update-time signature/version checks are already an RL-100 capability, and AS-17/AS-19 further confirm both the debug port and the bootloader's own storage are not intended to be left modifiable in production. The residual gap is the missing boot-time trust anchor, whatever residual strength REQC006's readout-protection implementation ultimately provides, and correct implementation of the signature-verification logic itself (REQC012).

threats.description: An attacker with physical proximity to the tank/process introduces a false radar reflection (e.g. foil, decoy target, signal reflector) so C-1 reports a plausible-but-wrong level.
threats.likelihoodRationale: Requires sustained physical proximity to the process without detection. AS-11 confirms the radar front-end performs basic plausibility/consistency checks, which raise the bar somewhat, but is not a dedicated anti-spoofing system, so a sophisticated attacker crafting a plausible reflection is not specifically countered.
threats.impactRationale: The value stays in-range, so AS-4/AS-5's fail-safe logic never triggers (no detected device fault); the full AS-A1 safety/integrity objective applies.
threats.classificationRationale: AS-11 confirms the radar front-end has no dedicated anti-spoofing capability (a product gap the manufacturer could improve), but the attack also requires sustained physical proximity to the tank/process, which is a plant access-control matter.
threats.deploymentConstraints: Requires the plant to restrict physical access to the tank/process area near the radar sensing path.

threats.description: An attacker with physical access to the external QSPI flash (C-6) reads out the firmware image.
threats.likelihoodRationale: AS-14 confirms the firmware image is not encrypted at rest on the external QSPI flash, so any attacker capable of reading the chip (a lower bar than full reverse-engineering) can extract it. AS-17's debug-port lockdown does not mitigate this vector: reading an external SPI flash chip directly (in-circuit or desoldered) does not require MCU debug access.
threats.impactRationale: A read-only extraction only exposes confidentiality, bounded by AS-A10's confidentiality objective; firmware integrity is unaffected since the update-time signature/version checks (AS-3) apply regardless of whether the image was read.
threats.classificationRationale: AS-14 confirms the firmware image is not encrypted at rest on the external QSPI flash; adding at-rest encryption is entirely within the manufacturer's control.
threats.acceptanceRationale: firmware itself does not hold much confidentiality; attack only possible in lab

threats.title: Malformed protocol input causes firmware crash, hang, or undefined behavior

costRationales.time: Effort required for this attack path.
costRationales.exploitability: Technical difficulty once the attack surface is reached.

threats.description: An attacker (or a malfunctioning peer) sends malformed/malicious frames to a protocol parser (HART, Modbus RTU, or the Ethernet service interface) that the firmware does not handle robustly, causing a crash, hang, or undefined behavior rather than a clean rejection of the frame.
threats.likelihoodRationale: Modbus RTU's shared multidrop exposure (AS-6) gives the lowest-bar attacker (the selected SL-C 2 attacker) a channel to send arbitrary malformed frames with no authentication needed; HART (the selected SL-C 2 attacker with physical access) and the Ethernet service interface (the selected SL-C 2 attacker with local access) face the same parser-robustness question over a smaller attack surface. Rated as a generic embedded-parser-robustness risk pending the dedicated fuzz/malformed-input test coverage required by REQC005, not as an assumption that the current parsers are known-broken.
threats.impactRationale: A crash/hang of the firmware/RTOS affects AS-A2's availability objective directly and, transitively, AS-A5's Modbus function -- a watchdog-triggered reset and restart still costs measurement/communication availability for the duration of the recovery, so availability impact stays at the ceiling (3). Safety impact is lowered from the initial conservative rating of 2 to 1: AS-18 now confirms an independent watchdog is assumed present and is intended to force the analog output to AS-4/AS-5's defined fail-safe fault current during the reset/restart sequence, rather than holding a stale value, so a firmware hang/crash/deadlock is designed to surface as a detectable device fault rather than a misleading measurement.
threats.classificationRationale: Protocol parser robustness against malformed/malicious input is entirely within the firmware implementation, addressed going forward by REQC005's mandatory fuzz-testing gate.

threats.description: A Maintenance/Service-credential holder deliberately clears the event/diagnostic log to conceal prior security-relevant actions (e.g. an earlier unauthorized configuration change or firmware update).
threats.likelihoodRationale: Clearing the log requires an existing Maintenance/Service credential (AS-1/AS-2), narrowing this to the same insider-type actor as T-15/T-18 rather than an arbitrary attacker; AS-16's design already ensures the clear action itself always creates a log entry, so full, undetectable evidence erasure is not possible with a single action.
threats.impactRationale: Impact is on forensic/accountability value rather than direct process control, bounded by AS-A11's objectives (confidentiality 1, integrity 2, availability 1, safety 0); AS-16's self-logging of the clear action is a built-in partial mitigation already reflected in this rating.
threats.classificationRationale: The log's self-logging-of-clear-events design (AS-16) is a product capability, but how tightly the plant restricts and vets who holds Maintenance/Service credentials is a deployment/governance factor that determines how likely a malicious-insider scenario actually is.
threats.deploymentConstraints: Requires the plant to restrict Maintenance/Service credential issuance to vetted personnel and, since the local circular log is not an audit-grade record (AS-16), to periodically export/archive the log off-device if long-term forensic retention is required.

threats.description: A compromised or malicious commissioning/engineering laptop (or an on-path adjacent attacker) exploits an implementation weakness in the TLS session setup for IF-4 -- e.g. incomplete certificate/hostname validation, acceptance of deprecated cipher suites, or a downgrade attack -- to intercept or tamper with an otherwise-intended-to-be-authenticated, encrypted session.
threats.likelihoodRationale: AS-8 commits IF-4 to an authenticated, encrypted transport, and REQC004 sets a concrete minimum bar (TLS 1.2+, device-unique certificate, tested cert/hostname validation, non-deprecated cipher suites). Residual likelihood reflects the generic implementation-risk class present in any TLS deployment (validation logic bugs, cipher downgrade) that REQC004's dedicated test coverage is intended to catch before release.
threats.impactRationale: Impact reflects AS-A13 (key material) since the session could expose key-management traffic, capped at AS-A13's confidentiality/integrity/safety objectives; AS-A6/AS-A14 are also exposed via the same session.
threats.classificationRationale: TLS implementation correctness (certificate/hostname validation, cipher suite negotiation) is entirely within the firmware's TLS stack integration, verified going forward via REQC004's test coverage requirement and REQC012's requirement to use a validated cryptographic library rather than a custom implementation.

threats.description: AS-19 confirms the production bootloader is stored in a write-protected region of MCU internal flash and cannot be modified through the normal firmware-update path. This threat covers bypass of that protection itself: via debug/JTAG access (IF-7) if MCU readout protection is defeated, via hardware fault injection against the flash-protection logic, or via compromise of the manufacturing/provisioning process where the bootloader and its root-of-trust material (firmware-signing key) are originally installed.
threats.likelihoodRationale: AS-19 confirms the bootloader itself is write-protected under the normal update path, closing the straightforward bootloader-overwrite scenario. Residual likelihood reflects only the harder bypass routes: defeating MCU readout/flash protection via debug access (the same the selected SL-C 2 capability effort as T-11/T-13's RDP-defeat scenario), fault injection against the protection mechanism (AS-13 confirms no dedicated fault-injection resistance, mirroring T-16's reasoning), or compromise of the manufacturing/provisioning process itself (bounded by REQC007's key-management policy).
threats.impactRationale: Bounded by AS-A2/AS-A10's integrity/safety objectives; a compromised bootloader can install and trust arbitrary application firmware, the most severe outcome in the update/boot trust chain.
threats.classificationRationale: The bootloader's write-protection (AS-19) and the manufacturing key-management policy (REQC007) are both entirely within the manufacturer's control; the debug-access and fault-injection bypass routes mirror T-11/T-13/T-16's existing reasoning about defeating hardware protections rather than being a new class of exposure.
